study_identification_part.si4_title: Neurofind: using deep learning to make individualised inferences in brain-based disorders

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: Introduce Neurofind, a freely available web tool that applies data harmonisation and normative modeling to structural MRI to compute an Outlier Index Score (deviation from normative morphology) and Brain Age; demonstrate exemplar applications in Alzheimer's disease and schizophrenia.

rci1_dataset_name.supporting_text: Data for training the web-based normative models used in Neurofind consisted of four publicly available datasets of healthy controls, namely the Human Connectome Project, the Human Connectome Project Aging, Biobank and IXI.

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: Neuroharmony method - a random forest model that learns the relationship between image quality metrics (IQMs) and ComBat corrections, then predicts and applies corrections for new unseen images; trained twice (with age+sex covariates for Outlier Detection model, with sex covariate only for Brain Age model); designed specifically for harmonizing images from unseen scanners; within-scanner outlier removal performed before harmonization
rci9_site_effect_handling.supporting_text: Scanner effects on the ROIrel were mitigated using the Neuroharmony method [56]. Briefly, Neuroharmony uses a random forest model to capture the relationship between IQMs and the corrections for each brain region prescribed by ComBat, a popular harmonisation approach that uses an empirical Bayes framework to correct for additive and multiplicative batch effects [68]. Once this relationship is learned, Neuroharmony predicts and applies the ComBat corrections for a new set of IQMs extracted from an unseen T1-weighted image. Neuroharmony was trained twice to accommodate the specific needs of the Outlier Detection and Brain Age models. For the former, Neuroharmony was trained whilst controlling for the effects of age and sex, whereas for Brain Age, only sex was added as a covariate.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: AD shows large deviations from normative morphology with many high outliers and homogeneous deviation patterns; SZ shows fewer extreme outliers and more heterogeneity; both groups exhibit accelerated brain ageing.
